author: Claude (English teacher role), v2 after expert audit
basis: Rewritten against the v2 quality gate after two independent expert audits (CEFR assessor; speech coach + fact checker) found the v1 text passed on averages while individual slides missed their band, A2 and B1 were the same sentences with synonyms swapped, and several facts had drifted. Facts corrected to source: +1.6 degrees over a century (NSTC 2024) against a global 1.3; Climate Change Response Act 2023; carbon fee live 2025; Taichung capture demonstration about 2,000 t/yr, not a deployed solution; public transport share is about 14%, so 'we rely on public transport' was removed; 'Silicon Shield' dropped as a cross-strait deterrence term unsuited to a climate talk. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count.

slides.1: Last summer Taiwan broke its own temperature record again. That was not bad luck. It was a warning, and today I will show you how we can answer it.
slides.2: SDG 13 is called Climate Action. It asks every country to cut carbon gas and to get ready for storms and flooding. That work has already started here.
slides.3: Think about where we live. Taiwan is a crowded island with many mountains, so typhoons and high seas reach us fast. Our big factories also need huge power.
slides.4: First, the bad news. Over one hundred years Taiwan warmed by 1.6 degrees, while the whole world warmed by 1.3. Scientists say our island is heating faster.
slides.5: Here is the main problem. Taiwan still burns coal and gas for most of its power, and our chip factories run day and night. Clean power must grow faster.
slides.6: So ask yourself two questions. Can a small island pay for all this energy? And if we keep burning coal, who will fix the damage later?
slides.7: Now the good news. In 2023 Taiwan passed a climate law that sets one target: net zero by 2050. Big polluters now pay a carbon fee too.
slides.8: You can see the change at sea. Hundreds of wind turbines now stand off our west coast. Solar panels cover school roofs, fish ponds and farm sheds.
slides.9: People help too. Taiwan recycles more than most countries, and many of us ride the MRT or a YouBike. But daily habits alone cannot stop this.
slides.10: Engineers want a smarter grid. The plan is to let computers move power to the places that need it most, minute by minute. Taipower is testing it now.
slides.11: Scientists are also trying carbon capture. At a power plant in Taichung they catch about 2,000 tonnes of carbon each year. It is small, but it is a start.
slides.12: Look at our streets. Taiwan makes electric scooters with a battery you can swap in ten seconds. Swap points now cover the whole island, from Taipei to Kenting.
slides.13: Green choices are not cheap. New machines cost money, and a small shop cannot always pay. A fair plan must help those shops, not punish them.
slides.14: Energy security is a hard choice. Our factories need steady power every hour, but wind and sun come and go. Should Taiwan pick gas, or nuclear?
slides.15: Weather does not stop at a border. Taiwan wants to share what we build, though we cannot join the big climate meetings. A storm does not check passports.
slides.16: Watch out for greenwashing. Some firms say they are green but change very little. Ask them one thing: what exactly will you do before 2050?
slides.17: So where are we now? Taiwan has passed the law, built the wind farms and started the first carbon tests. A coal-heavy island is slowly turning green.
slides.18: Why should you care? Because your choices about jobs, votes and everyday habits will shape the next thirty years. Young people move this country.
slides.19: You do not have to feel afraid. You do have to feel useful. Learn the science, question the numbers, and tell people whatever you discover.
slides.20: The clock is running, and the question is yours. Will you watch this change happen, or help to build it? Taiwan is ready for SDG 13, and so am I.
